t: 3460. Longest Common Prefix After at Most One Removal
o:
**Understanding the problem**
Given strings s and t, we may delete at most one character from s (or none) and want the longest common prefix length with t.

**Examples:** "madxa" vs "madam": they agree on "mad" (3 chars), then 'x'≠'a'; deleting s[3] aligns s[4]='a' with t[3]='a' giving 4. "leetcode" vs "eetcode": delete s[0] to get 7. Identical strings need no deletion. "a" vs "b" gives 0.

With lengths up to 10⁵ we need a linear two-pointer solution, not trying every deletion.
k: Find the first mismatch index i by direct comparison.
Deleting any s[k] with k ≤ i produces the same alignment afterwards: s[i+1:] against t[i:].
So the answer is i plus the length of the continued match of s[i+1:] with t[i:].

a.n: Approach 1: Two pointers around the first mismatch
a.i: All deletions at or before the first mismatch are equivalent, so it suffices to test the single alignment obtained by skipping s[i]. Continue matching s[j+1] with t[j] from j = i; the final j is the answer.
s: Advance i while s[i] == t[i] (bounded by both lengths).
If a string ended, return i (no deletion needed or possible improvement).
Otherwise resume matching with s shifted by one: advance j while s[j+1] == t[j].
a.t: O(|s| + |t|) — two sequential pointer sweeps, each character visited once.

a.n: Approach 2: Brute force over deletion positions
a.i: Try deleting each index k of s (and no deletion), computing the common prefix each time. Simple and obviously correct, but quadratic — fine only for tiny inputs; useful as a correctness oracle when testing the linear solution.
s: For each k from 0 to |s|−1, form the match count of s with s[k] skipped against t.
Also compute the no-deletion match count.
a.t: O(n²) — n candidate deletions, each with a linear prefix scan.

w:
**Wrap-up**
Always present the two-pointer solution; the brute force is only for explanation/stress-testing. Pitfalls: forgetting the no-deletion case (handled automatically since if no mismatch occurs we return early); assuming deleting from t is allowed (it is not); off-by-one in the shifted comparison s[j+1] vs t[j]. Follow-up: allow one removal from *either* string — run the same routine both ways and take the max.
